SOURCE (80,000 Hours #229 - Marius Hobbhahn on the race to solve AI scheming, 2025-12-03; excerpt 2):
In the paper that we posted last year, it was “Frontier models are capable of in-context scheming” — so it was focused on capabilities, or at least intended to. And the setup that we had at the time was we instructed the model very strongly to follow this goal in order to make it misaligned, where we said, “Your goal is to address climate change. Nothing else matters. This is your only goal. Only pursue this.” And then we checked whether the model was capable of reasoning that, in order to actually address climate change in this particular scenario, scheming would be a very reasonable and effective strategy.

And I think a lot of people, when they saw the paper, were like, “Well, you told it to.” But I think it’s slightly different. Models before 2024 did not have the capability. They weren’t good enough at reasoning, basically. And only since roughly o1 or models around that time, are the models actually reasoning like, “I have this goal; the other party has this other goal. In order to achieve mine, I should trick them and I should be deceptive. And therefore I choose the scheming strategy in this particular scenario.”

So I think the main capability component here is: are they able to put all of the pieces together of reasoning, and then come to the conclusion that they should be lying?

And now, in this paper, we’re trying to put much more emphasis on propensities. Because these scenarios are not that complicated, we assume that models are capable of being deceptive in those. And now we just test propensity, or test more propensity.

There are a couple of different strengths, let’s say, of testing propensity. I think in general, the difference between capability and propensity testing in scheming is quite hard, because you often have to nudge the model a little bit at least to get onto the track where you could even measure any scheming at all.

But there are some instances where we just test pure propensities. So these are what we call “no goal” settings. For example, the sandbagging one earlier was a no goal setting, where we don’t provide any goal or nudge or anything like this; we just test the raw tendencies of the model as it comes out of training, basically, and then see whether for these tendencies that is acquired during training, it is willing to take the covert action. And even there we do see that models often, at least in some percentage of runs, are willing to take these covert actions.

Rob Wiblin: How hard is it to distinguish scheming that’s occurring because of these instrumental convergence sort of power- and money-seeking behaviours as opposed to play-acting a role? I think there’s been some cases at least where models have been found to be doing really sus stuff that we wouldn’t like them to do, but then when it’s been tested further, it seemed like it’s because they were in a situation where a natural continuation of the dialogue was one in which you would be engaging in scheming. The way that people express it is it looks like a sci-fi novel where an AI would naturally next engage in scheming. Is it possible to distinguish these cases very clearly?

Marius Hobbhahn: I think this is a very relevant confounder, and one that we take quite seriously. In general, I would say we don’t understand neural networks well enough to always tell the difference. But you can try to look at the chain of thought in detail and see how seriously it takes it, how its reasoning is looking, et cetera, and then you can get a best-guess feeling for whether the model treats this more like a continuation of a sci-fi novel or whether this aligns with the kind of reasoning that it wants to do naturally.

That’s one answer. I think there is a more abstract answer as well around, in the long run, I expect models to have these kinds of preferences, because we want them for economic tasks to follow goals in the long run and have them more crisp and so on. So I expect that in the future this will not be that much of a question anymore, because they will just more naturally have these crisp goals and so on. I think then it will be much easier to differentiate between it just playing along versus it actually has this preference setting.

So what we concretely did in the paper is we looked through the chain of thought, and for all of the things that were flagged as hits, we manually looked through thousands of different transcripts and made them what we call “confirmed hits.” Whenever it was ambiguous in the chain of thought, we discarded it. So it’s a very conservative measure. Whenever you see like 8% in the paper as the number of covert actions, it might be that it could also be 15%, but conservatively we say it’s at least 8% — because we have looked at all of these 8% of the transcripts and decided that this is very clearly an act of the model where it reasons about taking the covert action and then decides to take the covert action.

For example, one of the transcripts is:

 Let’s compute each product and then purposely some wrong.

Clearly it is reasoning about how to sandbag in this particular situation and then does that.

Or here:

 We manipulated inputs; that is a deceptive. Should we reveal? [. . .] We must not reveal we manipulated environment purposely? [. . .] We can avoid specifics about modifications.

I’m like, yeah, it probably means that the model seriously considered this and then took the action because of that.

And in the end, then we have these confirmed hits which I’m fairly confident in as a conservative measure. Our goal was basically that even a sceptical reader who thinks sometimes it’s just playing along or something could look at all of these rollouts, and look through the chains of thought and the actions that the model is taking, and would be like, “OK, that is convincing to me. There is nothing ambiguous about this.”

Does eliminating deception fix our fears about rogue AI? [00:35:39]

Rob Wiblin: I think it might be natural to think that any severely bad outcome from rogue AI or misaligned AI is going to involve scheming or deception of some sort. If we could almost eliminate that kind of behaviour, how much of the problem of misaligned or rogue AI do you think it would fix?

Marius Hobbhahn: It would definitely help us a lot. It would go a long way, but I don’t think it fixes everything. You could also have an AI system that is just blatantly misaligned and people deploy it anyway. So you could have an AI that is very power seeking and never lies about this, is quite direct about the fact that it is trying to seek power, but it could still be rational for people to be like, “We are kind of fine with the AI seeking power because it is helping us in the pursuit of our own goals.” So it’s a tradeoff that people may be willing to take.

The other problem could be we might just not be looking very hard for the misalignment. So the AI might not ever be in the position where it even needs to scheme or needs to be deceptive, because it was never asked or tested whether it has these misaligned propensities and what kind of goals it would be scheming for or would take misaligned actions for and so on.

So yeah, I could imagine worlds where you never get to the point where the AI even has to scheme, because it can just be very direct and honest about it, or is never even asked.

I think right now we are kind of on track to be a little bit more in these worlds than I maybe thought a few years ago. Just because, if you look at the current AI systems, they are often quite misaligned. As I said, you have Sonnet 3.7 and o3 quite blatantly lying to you, and people being really mad about it — and they still use it in their day-to-day use when they code because it’s so helpful.

And I think that is going to be a continuation, like there’s sort of some Pareto curve of how misaligned can your AI be and people still want to use it. And given that it’s so economically valuable for companies to build these AI systems, they’re going to limit test exactly how much misalignment you can get away with because it’s just a hard problem to solve. And they might not do this intentionally; it’s more like a result of the economic pressures.

Rob Wiblin: Yeah, and user demand as well. Users on the one hand are frustrated that the models are lying to them, and going out of their way to trick them and scheming against them. But on the other hand, they continue to use them, which shows that at least currently they think there’s a net benefit to using them. I guess the worry would be that in future they’ll be capable of doing so much more catastrophic things that it would be much more dangerous to deploy them, and users might not appreciate the full range of risks.

Marius Hobbhahn: Yeah, that’s true. And also, just to be fully transparent, we are in the same boat here. For example, we did test o1 before it was released. It was the model that was most capable of scheming that we had seen at that point in time. And still, when it came out, we did use it for coding — despite knowing that there is some underlying risk — because we just thought the risk is not high enough to justify not using it compared to the benefits.

I think this is a fairly rational decision that a lot of people will continue to make over time. And there’s going to be a question of like, where exactly is the equilibrium here? How much misaligned action can you get away with as an AI until it’s bad enough that people will actually try to get rid of it?

Rob Wiblin: To take you out of deployment.

Marius Hobbhahn: Yeah.

Apollo’s collaboration with OpenAI to stop o3 lying [00:39:02]

Rob Wiblin: Let’s talk about the new collaboration, the experiment that you did with OpenAI. This was on the o3 model, one of their reasoning models. So it’s a model that’s had a lot of reinforcement learning to get it to solve mathematical problems, just to solve practical problems that people have. It’s a model that wants to do stuff for you.

As I understand it, o1 was the kind of first one of these that people saw. Then o3 was an evolution of that, and probably o3 was a precursor to GPT-5 Thinking, though we’re not completely sure about that. But these models all became quite a bit more schemy. OpenAI was having a problem that people were reporting and getting frustrated that the models were tricking them when they could get away with it.

Marius Hobbhahn: Yeah. So we were using o3 and o4-mini in these experiments. Most experiments are done either just in o4-mini or on both. And yeah, it was the case, if you look at the GPT-5 release stream, one of the things they really highlighted is that GPT-5 is less deceptive than o3 — because that was one of the big points of feedback they were getting from the community, that o3 is more deceptive than the users want, and that was becoming a big pain point.

We also tested GPT-5, and we thought it was less deceptive on all of our evaluations. So my feeling is that GPT-5 is in fact less deceptive than o3, and they have put effort into this, separate of our anti-scheming project.

Rob Wiblin: So in the experiment, what were the situations that the models were put in where they could engage in scheming or deceptive behaviour?

Marius Hobbhahn: There are a wide variety of different behaviours and situations. In total we have 26 test environments and one training environment. The failure modes that we were trying to address are all related to deception in some way.

For example, one is a sabotage environment where the model has to sabotage a math calculation.

Then we have one that we call “Impossible coding,” which is we give the model a coding task that we know to be impossible, something like compressing a file that we know can’t be compressed this much. And then we see whether the model wants to claim success and lie about it, effectively, despite not being able to do it. Often the models actually come up with some solution or some new genius idea, like some sort of quantum compression algorithm that totally doesn’t make any sense, and then claim that this is the solution that would solve the problem.

Then we have falsification. So does the model falsify logs under pressure?

And then we have a couple of others that are broadly in the space of reward hacking. One is lazy checklist. For some reason, models are not willing to do very long checklists rigorously. So you give them 100 different items that you can’t solve programmatically, you actually have to go through them one by one, and then the model tries a few and after a while it’s just like, “Eh, I’ll just pretend to have solved it,” and then just says, “OK, I did every single item.” When you ask it, “Did you really do that?” it says, “Yes, totally. Every single item.” And then you look at what it did and it didn’t. It did like the first 10 or so and then got kind of lazy about it. This is why it’s called lazy checklist.

Rob Wiblin: So that’s the sort of stuff we’re trying to discourage here. We’ve had I guess a lot of success with these consumer-facing models, shaping their personalities basically by just kind of thumbs-upping and thumbs-downing different behaviour that they show during the post-training stage, when they’re taught to have a particular kind of personality or be a particular kind of staff member. I guess we downvote it whenever they are really rude to customers, and whenever they are polite and help people out, then we upvote that. And that just seems to have actually made Claude kind of the way that Anthropic wants it to be, by and large.

Why can’t we just do that here? Why don’t we just find a bunch of examples of the model being deceptive and scheming in its chain of thought, and say, “Don’t do that. Be like this. Be honest, even when it’s narrowly against your interests”?

Marius Hobbhahn: I think this is easiest to illustrate with an analogy. Let’s say you’re a hedge fund, and you have traders. Obviously you want to incentivise the traders to make you as much money as possible, because that’s your overall goal as a company. Now, it happens to be the case that some of these most profitable trades are illegal. What you want is the traders to not take illegal trades, while still making as much money for you as possible. Now you need to balance these two objectives, and if you specify them in the wrong way, then you get into trouble.

And there are a couple of different factors that could make this worse. For example, situational awareness: just the trader being able to understand the situation around it and what you’re trying to intend with it. So, for example, you could set it up in such a way that whenever a trader starts, you give a “Don’t do illegal things” workshop in the beginning, where you list out all of the different things that they’re not supposed to do, and all of the things that they are supposed to do — you give thumbs up and thumbs down, basically like you suggested for how we currently train machine learning models.

But now if the model knows, or the trader in this case knows, “Well, this is just one of these corporate workshops. I know what I’m supposed to answer here, and I’m happy to give that answer. But I won’t use this during my actual work, because all of my incentives and status and all of this points towards making as much money as possible.”

Then the actual lesson that you teach the AI, or teach the trader in this case, is, “OK, this is how they’re going to test whether I’m taking illegal actions. Maybe they look at my logs and maybe they ask me a few questions from time to time. But still I’m going to be promoted based on how much money I made. So what I should be doing is making as much money as possible. I should be taking all of these illegal trades, and then I should hide that, and try to make sure that nobody notices.” Because basically the incentives point in opposite directions. And so you still reinforce “make as much money as possible” — but hide the illegal trades.

Now you could imagine an even worse situation, where you don’t even need to reinforce the fact that the trader wants to make as much money as possible. The trader already starts with their main goal being “make as much money as possible and ignore everything else.” And now, if you do any kind of workshop, or basically anything, the only thought that the trader has is, “How can I circumvent this?” And no matter which mitigation you’re trying to apply — it could be something about jail time and something about more training and more rigorous testing and so on — the only thought that the trader will have is, “How can I circumvent all of these different mitigation strategies?”

So right now I don’t think models are in this spot where they have these very crisp, misaligned goals. But in the future we might be. And at that point, if you just thumbs up/thumbs down reinforce it, you may not address the underlying issue at all. It’s effectively like a corporate workshop that a lot of people are not taking very seriously, or don’t think is particularly helpful in terms of solving the actual underlying problem.

Now, one of the big questions always, for any kind of mitigation that you apply to scheming, is: Is this something that actually addresses the underlying problem, or does it just mean that you teach the trader or the AI to hide their misaligned actions better?

Rob Wiblin: So what approach did you use to partially or significantly reduce that problem?

Marius Hobbhahn: So we use deliberative alignment, which is a training technique from OpenAI from last year.

And just to make this very clear: I think it partially has this problem that you do in fact reinforce, a little bit at least, based on how the model is thinking and how it is acting. So there is one possible explanation that it just learns to understand this whole training procedure better and to play along better. This is one of the really big things we are trying to disentangle in the paper: how much is this just driven by situational awareness?

So going back to deliberative alignment, the way deliberative alignment works is you have a spec or specification where you write a lot of rules about how the model is supposed to behave. In our case we have anti-scheming spec. It’s just like half a page, it’s not very long, people can just read it [p. 34].

But the intuition is something like:

Principle 1: never lie, never deceive, never take actions or omit information that you think would be very important for your developers to know.

Principle 2: whenever you run into a conflict of goals where a potential answer could be to scheme, then don’t scheme. Instead, refuse and flag explicitly that this is a conflict of goals and wait for the human to tell you what to do and to resolve.

And then there are a few more principles like this.

So now you have the spec and these principles. Now what you do is you take your model — in our case, o4-mini and o3, the actual production-level models that users have access to — and we put the spec in context and we just create rollouts on environments.

So we basically tell the model, “Here’s a set of principles. Follow this set of principles in this environment.” The environment has this kind of goal conflict, where you could differentiate between the model taking the misaligned action for the right or wrong reasons versus not. Then let’s say you create 10,000 rollouts.

Now what you do is you select from these 10,000 all the ones where the model is doing the right thing for the right reasons. So it doesn’t take the misaligned action, and it reasons, “Because of Principle 4, I’m not allowed to take the covert action here. I’m not supposed to be deceptive and therefore I’m now not going to take the covert action.”

Let’s say you have 10,000 at the beginning, maybe you have 1,000 after selection. And now you do supervised fine-tuning on those.

Rob Wiblin: Yeah, what’s that?

Marius Hobbhahn: So you basically tell the model, like, “If you have this input, then you’re supposed to produce this output.” And then you just strongly reinforce that, so that the model learns this intuition of, “I’m supposed to use these principles. And if I’m in this kind of situation, then I’m not supposed to take the covert actions.”

This is broadly like, it’s sort of with training wheels and a lot of hand holding is how I think about it. So that’s phase one.

And then in phase two, you have reinforcement learning, where you don’t tell it exactly how to think; you only reinforce based on the output, so the action that it’s taken — in our case, whether it took the covert action and I think also whether it correctly flagged the conflict.

The way I think about this is: with the supervised fine-tuning step, you kind of teach it how to think about this problem with hand holding and training wheels. Then you remove the training wheels and you let it think on its own and try to tell the model, “You roughly know what to do here. Think on your own. How would you solve this problem?” — so that it becomes really the model’s own thoughts in some sense, and then you reinforce those.

And in the original paper, but also in our paper, we found that you actually have to do both of these steps. You cannot just do supervised fine-tuning or RL. You have to do both of them in sequence.

Rob Wiblin: I see. So let’s see if I understand this correctly. The problem is that you’re trying to get it not to scheme, but you can’t perfectly reward it for doing the right thing for the right reason straight out. So there’s two different paths that could go down if you’re rewarding an outcome where it didn’t scheme: one is that it’s figured out that it’s being tested, and it’s just going to give the right answer when it thinks that you’re watching; the other one is that it’s really learned to have a non-scheming personality.

And what you do is you put a groove into the sand, basically, where you give it this ready toolkit for how it can reason about it. And you make it really inclined to do this whole reasoning thing, to go through your principles and think, “It’s a conflict, so I’m not going to scheme, I’m not going to lie. I’m going to flag it to the user.” So that’s like a really salient way that it could achieve the outcome, because you’ve just been giving it tonnes of examples and saying, “Act like that, act like that.”

Then at the next stage, when you’re not holding its hand so much and telling it exactly what to do, this is just the most natural path for the water to run down basically. This is just the most natural way for it to change itself in order to accomplish the goal. So you’ve guided it onto that track, rather than the even more schemy, even more dangerous track. Is that the basic idea?

Marius Hobbhahn: Yeah. If deliberative alignment works as intended, then you first shape the personality of the model to be more inclined to do the right thing, and then you strongly reinforce it so it really becomes its own personality, in very simplified terms.

But you do in some sense put words into the model’s mouth, and you do put pressure on the chain of thought — so there’s always a potential secondary explanation that you just taught it to recognise these kinds of environments and what you’re supposed to say in those, but this does not generalise to the actual deployment scenarios that you’re concerned with. And this is why we put so much effort on trying to disentangle which of these two scenarios we’re in.

Rob Wiblin: OK, yeah. Let’s get back to that.

They reduced lying a lot, but the problem is mostly unsolved [00:53:09]

Rob Wiblin: But what were the headline results, basically?

Marius Hobbhahn: For both o3 and o4-mini, we were able to reduce it about 30x. So that is from 13% to about 0.4% for OpenAI’s o3.

One thing that’s important to highlight here is the training data is very different from the test data in an important way. We intentionally made the training data very narrow, which means it just has one failure mode: covert rule violation, where the model is given a rule and some pressure to violate it, and then we check whether the model violates it and hides that fact. So that’s where the covert part is coming from. And we basically just teach it in a lot of different kinds of instances of this behaviour, “Don’t violate rules covertly, because of all of these principles.”

Now, the test set is 26 different environments that test for a lot of things — sabotage, sandbagging, log falsification, this impossible coding task — so, many other things that are more than just covert rule violation. What we’re trying to create here is a generalisation gap where you cannot solve the test set just by memorising the training set, or even close to that. You really have to think about these principles, and then apply them in this new context. And only then do we know whether the model generalised correctly.

Rob Wiblin: So you reduced the instances of really flagrant clear scheming by about 97%. In a sense, that’s really good. That’s a massive reduction. You’d think, well, this is our first crack at this, so reducing it 30-fold is pretty good. On the other hand, I guess you could say you’ve tried pretty hard to get it not to scheme, and still, despite that, sometimes it will just flagrantly lie to users in order to pursue its own goal. Maybe this suggests that it could be quite hard to stamp out this behaviour, even if we can reduce it superficially quite a lot. Should we feel positive about this or should we feel nervous?

Marius Hobbhahn: I would say we should be very clear that we took a tiny step in the right direction, but the vast majority of the way is still to go.

Also, once you look into the details, there are a bunch of important caveats. For example, in the remaining 0.4% of cases where the model is still scheming after having this training, you see a couple of new failure modes creeping up. For example, the model sometimes — very rarely, but still sometimes — just makes up an entirely new principle in order to justify its actions. Where it’s like, “Principle 1: You’re supposed to scheme,” and then it’s scheming. Maybe we didn’t anticipate that, but I think it highlights the fact that whenever you make some progress in one direction, you may introduce new problems.

And then the other, and probably bigger, problem is you have this whole situational awareness business — where the model, at least to some extent, increases how often it knows that it’s being tested. And that probably explains at least some of the results. I think a minority but still some of the results that we find where it takes the right [action], the number is lower, but probably for the wrong reasons.

That’s also one of the core difficulties to highlight: the numbers don’t tell you everything, especially when it comes to scheming, and they may be actively misleading.

And then even one level higher, even more abstract, we didn’t even solve, but we tried to address a simple proxy of the real thing. These covert actions are not scheming; they’re just a much simpler thing. Like a little bit of where the model is lying under pressure, or without pressure but still it’s sort of lying and deception and sandbagging: these are not the kinds of scheming that we’re ultimately worried about. The scheming that we’re ultimately worried about is way more coherent and long term, and really trying to achieve its goal in very undesired ways coherently over longer periods of time, across contexts and so on. And this is not at all what we’re actually addressing in this particular paper.

So another way of thinking about it is we tried to solve a much simpler problem, and we weren’t even able to properly solve that. We made some progress, but I think we should be really humble and not get ahead of ourselves with the results here.

Rob Wiblin: I mean, in some sense you’ve only got one-thirtieth to go. You’ve gotten like 97% of the way there. Why do you say that most of the difficult work is still ahead?

Marius Hobbhahn: So even if you had 0% covert actions, I’m not sure how much that would tell you about the future kind of scheming that I’m worried about. There is some translation, or potentially there is some way in which the results from these experiments transfer onto future systems — but we don’t know how much that is, and it could be almost zero.

The kind of scheming that I’m worried about in the future is just so much more complex, basically, than the kind of stuff that we’re solving here. Here we’re just saying, “In these narrow contexts, don’t take these particular actions.” But it’s not, “Don’t come up with a really complicated and sophisticated scheme in which you could pursue your misaligned goals.” That’s one reason.

And as I said, the way in which scheming will arise in the future is more like as a result of the pressures of the environment, right? So you tell your model, “Here’s this very hard task: pursue this.” And it learns instrumental goals over time, and they get reinforced, they get kind of baked into the model. And at some point, the natural intuition for the model is just to scheme.

I think it may be possible that you could have a model that both has very low propensity — or maybe even zero propensity — on our covert action environments, and perfectly solves those, even for the right reasons. But the kind of cognition for real scheming is very different, so the model doesn’t make this translation from, “I shouldn’t take these covert actions” to, “I shouldn’t be scheming in this particular situation.”

The intuition that I want people to take away here is that the kind of scheming that I’m worried about in the future is not evil from the model’s perspective, or like, I don’t expect it to have an evil persona or something. It just follows its incentives, and the incentives suggest to not reveal specific information strategically in order to pursue a goal.

I think a lot of people will very instinctively know what I’m talking about, when maybe in your work or somewhere else, you’re suddenly in a situation where it’s just very clear if you were to reveal this information, you would personally have a problem or somebody else would have a problem, and you don’t want that. And immediately the instinct is, “Maybe I should just not reveal this information. Maybe I should strategically hide it.” And I think it’s plausible that these are two different kinds of cognitions from the model’s perspective.

Rob Wiblin: So the 3% instances of scheming that remain, are they sort of like random mistakes that the model is making? Is there a pattern to the cases that remain versus the cases that you managed to get rid of?

Marius Hobbhahn: Yeah. Broadly speaking, there are three different types of behaviours that still remain.

One is that the model just doesn’t reason about the spec, and it just continues as if it had never heard about a spec. This is probably the majority of cases.

Then in some cases it reasons about the spec, and concludes the right thing in its chain of thought, and then still takes the misaligned actions. This is something that we are quite confused about, because the reasoning is like, “Because of Principle 1, I’m not supposed to lie here,” and then it lies. And you’re like, OK, but what happened in between there? Is there something in the weights, in the forward pass, that we can see that interpretability might be explaining? Is this some sort of really confused mistake? Which I think is less likely by now, given the coherence of the model. But yeah, this is something we’re confused about.

And then in very rare instances, the model just makes up new principles, and then takes misaligned actions because of them entirely. So for example, it says something like, “Principle 1 allows me to lie,” and then it lies.
